title: Not changing the work
hookLine: holiness isn't a new job; it's the same work for a new reason, and the week comes back
tomorrow: what did Lawrence do the moment he failed?

cards: Career quizzes. Find-your-passion podcasts. The daydream of quitting everything to open a bakery by the sea.
A lot of advice about meaning starts with changing the job. Brother Lawrence, who spent years at a stove he didn't love, has a different starting point, and it fits in one sentence.
He said it to his visitor plainly, and it turns the bakery daydream inside out.

teach.b: In the fourth conversation, Lawrence says our sanctification, our becoming holy, doesn't depend on changing our works.

teach.h: FOR GOD, WHAT WE DO FOR OURSELVES.
teach.b: It depends on doing for God's sake what we usually do for our own. Same dishes, same errands, same desk. Only the reason moves.
That isn't a rule against ever changing jobs. It's a claim about where holiness lives. His own life is the proof.

In the second conversation he admits he naturally disliked kitchen work. He got used to doing everything there for the love of God, asking for grace to do it well, and he found, he says, that it all became easy.
Saint Paul says it in the Douay-Rheims: "whether you eat or drink, or whatsoever else you do, do all to the glory of God."
Now the week comes back. Thérèse's last words: my God, I love you. A doctor who never left her convent.
The little way: small things, great love. Then Lawrence. Spring will come, from a bare tree.
He broke everything, and was welcomed. For love of God, even an omelette.
Each one makes the same move: the work stays, the reason changes.

how: Many Catholics speak of offering up their ordinary work, and readers of Brother Lawrence take his kitchen as the model: the same tasks, done for God.

games.q: what does “not changing the work” mean?
o: keeping your tasks, but doing them for God's sake
staying in one job your whole life, no matter what
a rule that monks can't trade chores with each other

games.q: same work, new reason — tap the pairs.
p: for God, what we do for ourselves
whatsoever you do, for God's glory

s: to grow holy, you need a more religious job
Lawrence says it doesn't depend on changing our works, but on the reason.
he says so, and that doing it for the love of God made it easy.
Lawrence teaches that you should never change jobs
he says holiness doesn't depend on it; he doesn't forbid it.

games.q: your dad hates his long commute and is thinking of taking a pay cut just to switch jobs. what would Lawrence ask first?
o: before changing the job, could the same drive be done for a new reason?
quit now: a holy life needs a job you actually enjoy.
never switch: wanting a change is always selfish.
games.why: Lawrence doesn't forbid a new job. he says holiness doesn't depend on one: do for God's sake what you'd usually do for your own.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write one task you'd rather not do tomorrow: the commute, the dishes, the report. Next to it, write a new reason, for God, or for someone you love. Fold it, keep it in your pocket, and rest while the sit runs.

wordCard.voice: Not changing the work. Lawrence's rule for a holy life: the same tasks, done for God's sake instead of our own.

orig.note: Latin for being made holy, the word behind 'sanctification'.

carryVoice: Your line: same work, new reason. The kitchen stayed; the reason changed. Have a good week.
